title: Fair dealing
hookLine: pay fairly, charge fairly, keep promises
tomorrow: first full paycheck, and a pay-in-four button. what's enough?

lines: A STRANGER'S CHANGE IN HER APRON.
cards: Payday at the stall comes in an envelope. Simran counts it at the bus stop and comes up one hour short: the extra hour she stayed to pack up when it rained.
And that same morning, a man paid with a twenty and walked off before she could hand him his change. It's still in her apron pocket. Two mistakes, one against her and one in her favor.
Her first thought: well, that's even.

teach.b: Not even, says the Sikh idea of fair dealing, because it runs in every direction: pay fairly, charge fairly, keep promises.
Guru Nanak makes the point with real force, on ang 141, and he does it by borrowing two neighbors' own deepest lines.

teach.h: ANG 141: ANOTHER'S DUE, LIKE A TABOO.
teach.b: In paraphrase: to take what rightfully belongs to another is like pork to a Muslim, and like beef to a Hindu.
Each listener hears the thing their own tradition most refuses, and the Guru says: that's how someone else's due should look to you.
The Punjabi word for that due is hakk, a person's rightful share. So the two mistakes don't cancel. They're two separate hakks.
The man's change is his. Simran seals it in an envelope with a note, tapes it inside the cash box, and tells Mrs. Ortega to watch for him next Saturday.
And the missing hour? Fair dealing isn't only not taking.
It's also asking, plainly, for what was agreed. She texts Mrs. Ortega: i think i'm missing an hour from the rainy Saturday.
No accusing, just the fact. Mrs.
Ortega writes back within a minute: my mistake, so sorry, I'll fix it this week. Two promises kept, one on each side of the stall. Nobody shaved.

how: Sikh teaching on work includes paying and charging fairly and keeping one's word; Guru Nanak's line on hakk, another's rightful share, is quoted on honesty in business.

o: splitting every bill exactly in half
bargaining hard so you always come out ahead

s: fair dealing only means not taking what isn't yours
it runs every way: pay fairly, charge fairly, keep promises, and ask plainly for what was agreed.
on ang 141, Guru Nanak compares another's due to what each listener's own tradition refuses
like pork to a Muslim and beef to a Hindu.
a mistake in your favor cancels a mistake against you
they're two separate hakks; each gets put right.

games.q: a friend borrowed forty dollars months ago and seems to have forgotten. you're quietly annoyed. going by today?
o: ask plainly and kindly, without accusing; fair dealing runs both ways.
let it go forever; asking for money back is never polite.
borrow forty from her sometime and just never mention it.
games.why: Simran asked for her missing hour with just the fact, no accusing. fair dealing includes asking for what was agreed.

practice: Bring to mind anything small you owe: a few dollars, a borrowed book, a reply you promised. If you can settle it now, do it: send the money, send the message.
If you can't yet, choose the exact time you will, and sit with it settled.

wordCard.voice: Fair dealing. Paying fairly, charging fairly and keeping promises, so no one's rightful share is taken.

orig.note: Punjabi: hakk, a person's rightful share; ang 141 warns against taking another's.

carryVoice: Your line: deal fairly. Nobody shaved and nobody shamed, on either side of the stall. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 141 (Majh ki Var, salok of Guru Nanak: hak paraaiaa naanakaa us suar us gaai), paraphrased
